content.heading: 6.1 Inner Product, Length, and Orthogonality
content.paragraph: Geometric concepts of length, distance, and perpendicularity, which are well known for $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ and $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, are defined here for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. These concepts provide powerful geometric tools for solving many applied problems, including the least-squares problems mentioned above. All three notions are defined in terms of the inner product of two vectors.
content.heading: The Inner Product
content.paragraph: If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, then we regard $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ as $n \times 1$ matrices. The transpose $\mathbf{u}^{T}$ is a $1 \times n$ matrix, and the matrix product $\mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{v}$ is a $1 \times 1$ matrix, which we write as a single real number (a scalar) without brackets. The number $\mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{v}$ is called the inner product of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, and often it is written as $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$. This inner product, mentioned in the exercises for Section 2.1, is also referred to as a dot product. If
then the inner product of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ is

It is clear from the calculations in Example 1 why $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}$. This commutativity of the inner product holds in general. The following properties of the inner product are easily deduced from properties of the transpose operation in Section 2.1. (See Exercises 29 and 30 at the end of this section.)

content.paragraph: Suppose $\mathbf{v}$ is in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$, say, $\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} a \\ b \end{array} \right\rbrack$. If we identify $\mathbf{v}$ with a geometric point in the plane, as usual, then $\parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel$ coincides with the standard notion of the length of the line segment from the origin to $\mathbf{v}.$ This follows from the Pythagorean Theorem applied to a triangle such as the one in Figure 1.

image.alt: A graph shows a right-angled triangle lying in the second quadrant with one of its vertices on the origin.

content.paragraph: A similar calculation with the diagonal of a rectangular box shows that the definition of length of a vector $\mathbf{v}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ coincides with the usual notion of length.
For any scalar $c$, the length of $c\mathbf{v}$ is $|c|$ times the length of $\mathbf{v}$. That is,
(To see this, compute $\text{∥}\textit{c}\textbf{v}\text{∥}^{2} = (c\mathbf{v}) \cdot (c\mathbf{v}) = c^{2}\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} = c^{2}\text{∥}\textbf{v}\text{∥}^{2}$ and take square roots.)

A vector whose length is $1$ is called a unit vector. If we divide a nonzero vector $\mathbf{v}$ by its length—that is, multiply by $1/\text{∥}\textbf{v}\text{∥}$—we obtain a unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ because the length of $\mathbf{u}$ is $\left( 1/\text{∥}\textbf{v}\text{∥} \right)\text{∥}\textbf{v}\text{∥}$. The process of creating $\mathbf{u}$ from $\mathbf{v}$ is sometimes called normalizing$\mathbf{v}$, and we say that $\mathbf{u}$ is in the same direction as $\mathbf{v}$.
Several examples that follow use the space-saving notation for (column) vectors.

content.heading: Distance in ℝn
content.paragraph: We are ready now to describe how close one vector is to another. Recall that if $a$ and $b$ are real numbers, the distance on the number line between $a$ and $b$ is the number $|a - b|$. Two examples are shown in Figure 3. This definition of distance in $\text{ℝ}$ has a direct analogue in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.

content.heading: Orthogonal Vectors
content.paragraph: The rest of this chapter depends on the fact that the concept of perpendicular lines in ordinary Euclidean geometry has an analogue in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.

Consider $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ or $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ and two lines through the origin determined by vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$. The two lines shown in Figure 5 are geometrically perpendicular if and only if the distance from $\mathbf{u}$ to $\mathbf{v}$ is the same as the distance from $\mathbf{u}$ to $- \mathbf{v}$. This is the same as requiring the squares of the distances to be the same. Now

image.alt: A figure shows vectors u, v, and negative v as the three vertices of a triangle.

content.paragraph: The same calculations with $\mathbf{v}$ and $- \mathbf{v}$ interchanged show that
The two squared distances are equal if and only if $2\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = - 2\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$, which happens if and only if $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$.

This calculation shows that when vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are identified with geometric points, the corresponding lines through the points and the origin are perpendicular if and only if $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$. The following definition generalizes to $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ this notion of perpendicularity (or orthogonality, as it is commonly called in linear algebra).

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ are orthogonal (to each other) if $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$.

content.paragraph: Observe that the zero vector is orthogonal to every vector in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ because $\textbf{0}^{T}\mathbf{v} = 0$ for all $\mathbf{v}$.

The next theorem provides a useful fact about orthogonal vectors. The proof follows immediately from the calculation in (1) and the definition of orthogonality. The right triangle shown in Figure 6 provides a visualization of the lengths that appear in the theorem.

image.alt: A figure shows a tilted right-angled triangle and line segment meeting one of the triangle's vertices at point 0.

note.title: Theorem 2
note.heading: Theorem 2
The Pythagorean Theorem
note.paragraph: Two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are orthogonal if and only if $\text{∥}\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\text{∥}^{2} = \text{∥}\textbf{u}\text{∥}^{2} + \text{∥}\textbf{v}\text{∥}^{2}$.

content.heading: Orthogonal Complements
content.paragraph: To provide practice using inner products, we introduce a concept here that will be of use in Section 6.3 and elsewhere in the chapter. If a vector $\textbf{z}$ is orthogonal to every vector in a subspace $W$ of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, then $\textbf{z}$ is said to be orthogonal to$W$. The set of all vectors $\textbf{z}$ that are orthogonal to $W$ is called the orthogonal complement of $W$ and is denoted by $W^{\bot}$ (and read as “$W$ perpendicular” or simply “$W$ perp”).

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Let $W$ be a plane through the origin in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, and let $L$ be the line through the origin and perpendicular to $W$. If $\textbf{z}$ and $\textbf{w}$ are nonzero, $\textbf{z}$ is on $L$, and $\textbf{w}$ is in $W$, then the line segment from $0$ to $\textbf{z}$ is perpendicular to the line segment from $0$ to $\textbf{w}$; that is, $\textbf{z} \cdot \textbf{w} = 0$. See Figure 7. So each vector on $L$ is orthogonal to every $\textbf{w}$ in $W$. In fact, $L$ consists of all vectors that are orthogonal to the $\textbf{w}$’s in $W$, and $W$ consists of all vectors orthogonal to the $\textbf{z}\text{’s}$ in $L$. That is,

content.paragraph: Remark: A common way to prove that two sets, say $S$ and $T$, are equal is to show that $S$ is a subset of $T$ and $T$ is a subset of $S$. The proof of the next theorem that $\text{Nul~}A = \left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$ is established by showing that $\text{Nul~}A$ is a subset of $\left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$ and $\left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$ is a subset of $\text{Nul~}A$. That is, an arbitrary element $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{Nul~}A$ is shown to be in $\left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$, and then an arbitrary element $\textbf{x}$ in $\left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$ is shown to be in $\text{Nul~}A$.

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix. The orthogonal complement of the row space of $A$ is the null space of $A$, and the orthogonal complement of the column space of $A$ is the null space of $A^{T}$:

content.heading: Proof﻿
content.paragraph: The row–column rule for computing $A\textbf{x}$ shows that if $\textbf{x}$ is in $\text{Nul~}A$, then $\textbf{x}$ is orthogonal to each row of $A$ (with the rows treated as vectors in $\left. \text{ℝ}^{n} \right)$. Since the rows of $A$ span the row space, $\textbf{x}$ is orthogonal to $\text{Row~}A$. Conversely, if $\textbf{x}$ is orthogonal to $\text{Row~}A$, then $\textbf{x}$ is certainly orthogonal to each row of $A$, and hence $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$. This proves the first statement of the theorem. Since this statement is true for any matrix, it is true for $A^{T}$. That is, the orthogonal complement of the row space of $A^{T}$ is the null space of $A^{T}$. This proves the second statement, because $\text{Row~}A^{T} = \text{Col~}A$.
